column4: The section says Imran's wife dedicated what was in her womb; this preceding verse gives her vow, “مَا فِي بَطْنِي مُحَرَّرًا.” It supplies why the sex of the child matters in the next ayah, 3:36.

The source section labels ذ ك ر's dictionary sense as a male child and recalls the old birth formula “أيسرت وأذكرت.” Mary instead says “وَضَعْتُهَا أُنثَىٰ,” then the verse distinguishes الذكر from الأنثى; the scene lets the reader hear that inherited ranking beside this particular birth.

The source section connects ربّ (root ر ب ب) with staged nurturing and a caregiver. Here her Lord “وَأَنبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا” and entrusts her to Zakariyya, showing the girl welcomed and raised well after the old formula had treated a male birth as the favorable outcome.

The source section's dictionary wording for childbirth is وَضَعَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ الْحَمْلَ; this verse says pregnant women's term ends when they “يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ,” then promises “يُسْرًا.” It joins the carried pregnancy, its laying down, and ease in one legal context.

The source section distinguishes حمل (pregnancy) from the written form حِمْل (a load). This verse says a mother “حَمَلَتْهُ” and “وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهًا,” making the physical carrying and painful delivery explicit.

The source section's birth dictionary form is وضع الحمل, the carried thing set down. At the Hour “وَتَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا”; the same childbirth action becomes a sign of terror rather than ordinary relief.
The source section compares a burden carried with a pregnancy carried. Mary “فَحَمَلَتْهُ” and withdraws with it, giving that comparison a concrete pregnancy scene before the labor in 19:23.
The section explicitly recalls this birth: labor (“الْمَخَاضُ”) brings Mary to a palm trunk. The scene anchors its language of carrying and setting down in the pain of an actual delivery.

The source section describes pregnancy as a burden that is carried and eventually set down. Here the wife “حَمَلَتْ حَمْلًا خَفِيفًا” and later both parents ask for a sound child, showing pregnancy as a changing, shared human concern.

The source section links load-bearing with birth; this verse describes a mother carrying her child “وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ” and then nursing/weaning him for two years. It extends the image from delivery into maternal care.

The section places birth, breastfeeding, hardship, and ease together. This verse regulates nursing and weaning and says “لَا تُضَارَّ وَالِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِهَا,” making the child's dependence and the mother's bodily burden a concrete duty of care.

The section's dictionary discussion pairs عسر with birth and later discusses nursing. Here “وَإِن تَعَاسَرْتُمْ فَسَتُرْضِعُ لَهُ أُخْرَىٰ” makes difficulty between parents a breastfeeding problem with a practical alternative.

The source section's root ع س ر / ي س ر concerns hardship and ease. This verse promises “بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا” in a passage about provision according to means, giving the birth-and-care sequence an explicit assurance of relief.

This neighbor to the labor in 19:23 contributes reassurance and provision: Mary is told “أَلَّا تَحْزَنِي” and that her Lord has placed a stream below her. The following 19:25 completes the immediate care with dates; this ayah supplies comfort during the birth scene.
Continuing the birth scene of 19:23–24, this ayah tells Mary to shake the palm trunk so fresh dates fall (“رُطَبًا جَنِيًّا”). Its own contribution is food provided to the mother at delivery.

The source section describes a folk blessing that wished for an easy male birth and a curse tied to a girl. This verse says God “يَهَبُ لِمَن يَشَاءُ إِنَاثًا,” placing daughters within God's gift rather than treating them as an ill outcome.

The source section names ذ ك ر as a male child in its secondary dictionary sense. This verse names both “ذُكْرَانًا وَإِنَاثًا” as gifts and also names barrenness, placing sex and fertility within God's measure rather than the old male-favoring birth formula.

The source section develops birth and the growth of a child; this verse says God creates people in their mothers' wombs “خَلْقًا مِّن بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ” within three darknesses. It makes hidden, staged development perceptible.

The section moves from pregnancy to a child being received and raised. This ayah says God forms people in wombs “كَيْفَ يَشَاءُ,” connecting the sexed birth scene to divine knowledge and formation before birth.

The section's womb-and-birth image includes what is carried and what is born. This verse says God knows what each female carries and what wombs “تَغِيضُ” or increase, giving the hidden changes of pregnancy a measure known to God.

The source section's dictionary verb وضع names giving birth. This verse says no female conceives or “تَضَعُ” except with God's knowledge, directly joining pregnancy, delivery, and what is hidden from human observers.

The section connects pregnancy to a carried thing that develops before birth. This verse places the drop “فِي قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ,” naming the womb as a secure lodging and giving the carrying image its protected setting.

The source section defines التربية (root ر ب ب) as developing something stage by stage to completion. This verse recounts the embryo's stages and its development “خَلْقًا آخَرَ,” a direct bodily counterpart to that dictionary description.

The section links pregnancy, birth, and gradual growth. This verse describes formation in the womb through stages and then being brought out as an infant, showing the transition from hidden carrying to birth.

The source section's dictionary form التربية (root ر ب ب) means development by stages to completion. This verse traces the human from a drop to an infant, maturity, and old age, spelling out that gradual passage.

The section follows birth into a child's care and growth. This verse says people are brought from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight, and hearts; its contribution is the newborn's beginning and subsequent capacity.

The source section labels ذ ك ر as a secondary dictionary sense for a male child and places it beside female birth. This verse names God’s creation of “الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَىٰ” from the paired reproductive process, making both sexes part of the same created order.

The source section records an old birth formula that favored a male child over a girl. This verse says God made “الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَىٰ,” placing male and female together as the two forms produced from the reproductive process.

The source section's dictionary form التربية (root ر ب ب) describes raising step by step. This prayer asks mercy for parents “كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا,” naming childhood care as a debt answered with care.

The source section connects ربّ (root ر ب ب) with nurture. God says of infant Moses “وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي,” making divine protection through childhood a counterpart to the section's image of the Lord who raises.

The section notes the source-surah's opening question and contrasts God's reassurance with Pharaoh's reproach. Pharaoh asks “أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا,” claiming to have raised Moses as an infant; the same root of nurture becomes a weapon for asserting control.

The section explicitly compares the remembered-care question with the preceding surah. This verse asks “أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَآوَىٰ”; its own contribution is God's sheltering of the orphan, a concrete memory of care behind reassurance.

The section places breastfeeding and a caregiver among its birth images. This verse says wet nurses had been forbidden to Moses before his sister offered a way to find a nurse, making infant feeding part of the story's care problem.

Continuing 28:12, this verse returns Moses to his mother “كَيْ تَقَرَّ عَيْنُهَا وَلَا تَحْزَنَ.” It completes the nursing episode with maternal reunion, linking feeding to the attachment and care after birth.

The source section explicitly labels رَبِيبَة as a caregiver/child-care word from root ر ب ب. This verse names “رَبَائِبُكُمُ اللَّاتِي فِي حُجُورِكُم,” stepdaughters under one's care, giving that secondary family-and-guardianship sense a Qur'anic setting.

The source section's dictionary account of التربية (root ر ب ب) is gradual growth toward completion. Here the Lord protects the treasure for two orphan boys “أَن يَبْلُغَا أَشُدَّهُمَا,” tying guardianship to the children reaching maturity.

The section develops child-rearing through its root ر ب ب and caregiver sense. This verse requires testing orphans until they reach marriageable maturity before handing over their property, a specific legal form of care through growth.

The section links the new-born sheep (dictionary form الرُّبَّى, root ر ب ب) with childbirth and also discusses male/female birth. This verse names sheep and goats, then asks about males, females, and what the females' wombs contain, joining the flock to sexed birth and human claims about it.

This neighbor continues the livestock argument from 6:143 with camels and cattle and again asks what their wombs contain. Its own contribution extends the sex-and-womb test from sheep and goats to other herd animals.

The source section's dictionary form يَسَرَتِ الْغَنَمُ (root ي س ر) describes a flock increasing in milk and offspring. This verse points to cattle, drink from their bellies, and their many benefits, giving the milk side of that livestock abundance a Qur'anic scene.

The source section uses flock milk as a secondary dictionary sense of ي س ر. This verse describes drinkable milk coming from livestock bellies, a specific bodily source for the abundance image rather than merely a shared word.

The source section explains ي س ر with ease and making something ready. God says “وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ,” presenting ease as preparation by the speaker, a close parallel to reassurance that ease accompanies hardship.

The source section's root ي س ر carries ease and facilitation. This verse promises “فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ,” so ease is a path someone is made ready for, not only a condition after a difficulty.

The source section pairs عسر and يسر in childbirth. In the fasting passage God says “يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ بِكُمُ الْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ الْعُسْرَ”; this repeats the same ease/hardship boundary in a different legal setting.
The source section defines وِزْر as a heavy load of sin. This verse's “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ” makes that moral burden explicit and says each bears their own.
The source section labels the surah's وِزْر as a heavy sin-load. This verse says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ,” specifying the moral boundary on who can bear such a load.

The source section's dictionary definition of وِزْر is a heavy burden of sin. This verse repeats that no bearer carries another's burden, making the moral load distinct from the pregnancy sense of حَمْل discussed beside it.
The source section calls وِزْر a heavy load of sin. This verse repeats “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ,” sharpening personal accountability beside the image of one thing carried and set down.

The source section identifies وِزْر as a load of sin. This verse states that one bearer does not bear another's burden, a moral use of load-bearing that clarifies why the surah's burden is no pregnancy.

The source section says وِزْر is the heavy load of sin. This verse says opponents will carry “أَوْزَارَهُمْ كَامِلَةً” and burdens from those they misled, giving the load a consequence that extends beyond the carrier.

The source section defines وِزْر as a weighty sin-load. This verse says one who turns away from the Reminder will carry “وِزْرًا” on the Resurrection Day, giving that secondary sense a precise judgment scene.

The source section notes that حِمْل (load) and حَمْل (pregnancy) share written letters while meaning differs. This neighboring verse calls the judgment load “حِمْلًا,” making the lexical distinction concrete beside 20:100's وِزْرًا.

The source section describes a sin as a heavy thing carried. This verse says opponents will bear their own “أَثْقَالَهُمْ” and additional burdens for those they misled, showing moral weight accumulated through action.

The source section describes وِزْر as a heavy sin-load and the surah itself pictures a load weighing on the back. This verse says people carry their burdens “عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ,” making the moral weight bodily visible.
The section's load is something carried and then removed. This prayer asks God “وَلَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا,” naming the opposite movement: do not impose a heavy burden on us.

The source section's word وضع describes setting down the carried burden. This verse says the Messenger “يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ,” a direct reversal in which burdens and shackles are removed from people.

The section sets an old preference for male birth beside the Qur'anic girl born to Imran's wife. This verse shows the contrary response to a daughter: the father's face darkens at the news, exposing the social devaluation the section's birth formula preserves.

Continuing 16:58, this verse shows the father hiding from people and weighing humiliation against burying the child. It supplies the consequence of the darkened face, a stark reversal of the good acceptance and care in 3:37.

The section's birth scene distinguishes girl from boy and questions the old curse attached to a girl. This verse brings the buried-alive girl before the judgment, reversing that valuation by making her the one who is asked.

Continuing the questioned buried girl of 81:8, this verse asks “بِأَيِّ ذَنبٍ قُتِلَتْ.” Its contribution is to name the killing as an injustice, the opposite of the section's old curse wishing a girl a hard birth.

The source section recalls the birth saying that treated a male child as favorable and a girl as a curse. This verse describes a man darkening with anguish when given news of a daughter, a direct social reversal to the acceptance in 3:37.

The source section notes ذ ك ر as a male-child word and records a birth blessing that preferred boys. This verse asks “أَلَكُمُ الذَّكَرُ وَلَهُ الْأُنثَىٰ,” exposing the unequal allocation of male and female that underlies that preference.

This neighbor concludes the question in 53:21 by calling it “قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزَىٰ,” an unfair division. It makes the gender hierarchy itself the problem, clarifying the section's contrast between inherited preference and God's raising of a girl.

The source section pairs عسر with يسر as hardship and ease, including birth phrases that reverse each other. This verse says “فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ,” the contrary direction to ease in 92:7 and a specific reversal of the section's ease promise.

Immediately after the section's scene of Mary being accepted and raised, Zakariyya asks his Lord for good offspring. This ayah's own contribution is the request for a child after he witnesses Mary's provision; it extends the birth-and-care scene into a prayer for offspring.

Continuing Zakariyya's request in 3:38, this ayah announces Yahya to him. Its own contribution is the promised male child, carrying the section's childbearing scene and male-child wording forward into the next moment of the same passage.

This ayah has Zakariyya ask how he could have a boy in old age when his wife is barren. It completes the childbearing difficulty behind the announcement in 3:39, giving the section's hardship/ease and male-birth details a concrete fertility parallel.

In the same surah as Mary's labor scene, Zakariyya describes his failing strength and white hair before asking for a child in 19:5. This ayah contributes bodily frailty as the setting for a difficult, late-life birth request.

Zakariyya asks his Lord for a successor and says his wife is barren; the following 19:7 announces a boy. This is a specific childbearing difficulty and divine provision parallel to the section's births and its movement from hardship to ease.

This ayah asks that the requested child inherit Zakariyya and the family of Jacob, extending the childbirth request in 19:5 into care and succession. It adds the future role of the child to the section's wordplay about a newborn and the root ر ب ب's nurturing sense.

This ayah announces Yahya as a son to the aged Zakariyya and barren wife from 19:4–5. Its own contribution is the promise of a child despite those obstacles, a direct instance of ease following reproductive hardship.

Zakariyya asks how he can have a boy when he is old and his wife barren. This ayah states the obstacle from his perspective; 19:9 supplies God's answer, so the row's contribution is the felt difficulty of the promised birth.

Continuing Mary's delivery scene after the reassurance and dates in 19:24–26, this ayah presents the infant Jesus in the cradle while people challenge Mary. Its own contribution is the newborn and his mother's public encounter, extending the section's delivery image into infancy.

Before the darkened face and threatened burial in 16:58–59, this ayah says the people assign daughters to God while reserving what they desire for themselves. Its own contribution is the gendered hierarchy that frames the section's old birth blessing favoring boys.

This ayah asks whether God has taken daughters from what He creates while selecting sons for the people; 43:17 then shows their face darkening at daughter-news. The present ayah supplies the male-over-female allocation that makes the next reaction intelligible.

The section recalls a traditional birth formula favoring male offspring. This ayah challenges the same preference in a theological reversal, asking whether God selected sons for people and took females from among the angels.

The section's old formula treated a male child as the favorable birth. This ayah challenges the inverse allocation of daughters to God and sons to people, exposing the unequal valuation behind that formula.

The section names ذ ك ر as a secondary dictionary sense for a male child and describes a birth blessing that favored boys. This ayah asks whether daughters belong to the Lord while the people take sons, another direct exposure of that sex hierarchy.

This ayah asks whether God chose daughters over sons. Its own contribution is to name that ranking as the disputed claim, a repeated gendered reversal related to the section's old male-favoring birth formula.
